name: Double Free
principle: The program calls free(), delete, delete[], or an equivalent release routine twice on the same memory address. The second release corrupts allocator metadata and can cause crashes, overlapping allocations, write-what-where, or code execution.
detection_signals: same pointer variable reaches two free(ptr), delete ptr, or delete[] ptr calls without ptr = NULL or reassignment between them
free(ptr) in an error branch followed by free(ptr) in a shared cleanup label or function epilogue
goto cleanup path frees ptr after an earlier early-exit branch already called free(ptr)
custom destructor/release API such as destroy_x(x), release_x(x), cleanup_x(x) frees an object, then caller also calls free(x) or delete x
object destructor deletes a member pointer and another method or cleanup path deletes the same member pointer
loop calls free(ptr) on an invariant pointer and the loop body does not assign ptr = malloc(...) or ptr = NULL
signal handler or asynchronous callback calls free(ptr) on storage also freed by the main control flow
negative_signals: free(ptr); ptr = NULL; occurs before any later free(ptr)
two release calls are in exclusive if/else branches that cannot both execute
between releases there is ptr = malloc(...), ptr = calloc(...), ptr = realloc(NULL,...), or new assigning a fresh allocation
code uses std::unique_ptr, std::shared_ptr, std::vector, std::string, or RAII ownership instead of manual delete/free
release function accepts a pointer-to-pointer and sets *p = NULL after freeing, e.g. free_x(&p)
false_defense_traps: checking if (ptr) before both free(ptr) calls without setting ptr = NULL after the first free
assuming free(ptr) changes ptr to NULL automatically
setting only a local alias to NULL while other aliases still point to the freed address
making a custom destroy() return early on NULL but not clearing the caller's pointer
using reference counting without atomicity or consistent ownership rules
verification_focus: Can one concrete allocation address reach more than one actual deallocation call without an intervening ownership transfer, reallocation, or NULL guard that prevents the second deallocation?

consequence_chains.trigger: signal handler frees memory also freed by interrupted normal code
allocator metadata is corrupted and later malloc returns overlapping or attacker-controlled chunks
consequence_chains.consequence: write-what-where and possible arbitrary code execution

consequence_chains.trigger: code dereferences the pointer after the first free and before or after the second free
consequence_chains.consequence: use-after-free with memory corruption or information disclosure

patch_principle: Give each allocation a single owner responsible for exactly one release.
After free/delete in C-style ownership code, clear the owning pointer and all reachable owner fields to NULL.
Centralize cleanup in one path and make error paths transfer control there without pre-freeing the same pointer.
Use RAII, std::unique_ptr, std::shared_ptr, containers, or automatic memory management where possible.
Make custom destroy/release functions idempotent via pointer-to-pointer APIs or explicit ownership state.
